doc.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

chapter: Creative ambitions and the jazz business
title: Festival audiences and creativity within older styles
summary: Jazz party audiences like the familiar; Davern, Vache and Hamilton show older styles can be personal voices.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well you probably wouldn’t get a very sympathetic ear at this particular festival if you were to try to do some of that.
Yeah. And I understand that and it’s fine.
In fact I remember last night just hearing comments around me. These people, they certainly know what they like.
And if you go a little above their heads, they’ll just say things like, “oooh, that went right through my head” or something. I hear these little bits and pieces.

Yeah. And I mean that brings up another kind of interesting facet is this whole idea, which I’ve really had to face, of playing older styles which are really basically formed. Like these styles are set, but to try to play it, I mean like here is, okay I have this career, this is what I do. Is it possible to do it in a creative way and in a personal way? And I have come to the belief that yes it is. I don’t mean to hold myself as a great example, but people like Kenny Davern, Warren Vache, Scott Hamilton, to me they’re very personal voices. They don’t sound like a copy of anybody else. You can’t say Kenny Davern is a clone of Pee Wee Russell or Benny Goodman. He sounds like Kenny Davern. And yet he’s playing now in the style that was kind of set decades before. He’s still creative and he’s still — I mean there’s a way of doing it. And I think that’s valid too. And I think some critics seem to be aware of that and others aren’t. But I mean that’s a difficult thing to pull off.
